en: Thereafter, for the sake of the *jñānasūtra* and so forth, having mentally established the maṇḍala circle in the sky above the site of the maṇḍala and having worshipped it, one who possesses the yoga of the Lord of the Maṇḍala, facing east, should take five threads of five [colors] each—either spun by a virgin with unbroken grains or purchased from a hero—and place them in five vessels. These have been dyed individually with white, yellow, red, dark green, and black fragrant pigments mixed with powdered white mustard seeds, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and the five medicinal herbs.
Having placed them in the palm of the left hand, starting from the tips of the fingers up to the base of the thumb...

Following that, for the purpose of the *jñānatilaka* and so forth, one mentally constructs the mandala circle in the space above the site of the mandala and makes perfect offerings. Then, facing east and endowed with the yoga of the Lord of the Mandala (*maṇḍaleśvara*), one takes five sets of five threads—either woven by an unblemished young maiden or purchased at the price of a hero—and places them in five vessels.

Those who remain should color [the substances] individually with fragrant powders of white, yellow, red, green, and black, mixed with mustard seed flour and the five nectars; then, they should arrange them in the palm of the left hand, starting from the tips of the fingers up to the thumb.

Having visualized the wisdom threads (*jñānasūtra*)—produced from the syllables *brūṃ*, *āṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*—which have arisen as the five Tathāgatas and are established in the hearts of the five Tathāgatas who comprise the respective directions placed in the sky, and which are produced from the syllable *vuṃ* and so forth and are accompanied by rays of light; one should then entreat Vairocana with this: "Oṃ āḥ! O Śāśvata, grant me the vajra-thread for the purpose of laying out the great maṇḍala, hūṃ! One should likewise entreat Ratnasambhava and the others, substituting their respective names.

Visualize that one has become the nature of the five Tathāgatas generated from the syllables *bhrūṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*. Then, having invited the Tathāgatas of their respective directions to reside in the sky, imagine that they dissolve into oneself. Within the hearts of the five Tathāgatas, visualize the wisdom threads formed from the syllables *bhrūṃ* and so forth, together with rays of light.

With "oṃ āḥ śā śvata vajrasūtram me prayaccha mahāmaṇḍalasūtraṇāya hūṃ," one should make this supplication to Vairocana; having completely transformed the name, it applies to Ratnasambhava and the others as well.

Having transformed the two eyes into the nature of yellow moons and suns arising from the syllable *jaḥ*, and having uttered "Oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyaṅkuśi jaḥ," one should—by means of a blazing gaze like a hook with eyes that dart and move and lashes drawn back—draw in those [deities] sent forth by Vairocana and the others, and cause them to enter within their respective colors upon the threads held in the hands. *oṃ dīptadṛṣṭyaṅkuśi jaḥ* (Having made the two eyes of the nature of moons and suns born from the syllable *jaḥ*: Oṃ, blazing gaze, hook, *jaḥ*).

Reciting these words, with eyes flickering rapidly as they lift and draw in the lashes, one should visualize that by means of a blazing gaze like a hook, Vairocana and the others are exhorted and dissolve into the colored threads held in one's hands.
Therefore, they consist of the five gnoses, such as the mirror-like [gnosis] and so forth; thus, there are threads differentiated by a hundredfold divisions.

Then, together with a disciple who holds the thread and assumes the form of Vairocana or another [deity] such as Vighnāntaka, one should first wind each of the five sets of five threads individually. Subsequently, having formed a single thread from those five that have been wound in that manner, [one recites]: *oṃ āḥ* all phenomena follow one another; all phenomena have entered into one another; all phenomena have entered into one another completely; *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*.

Uttering this, the preceptor, having inserted the index finger—starting from the index finger and including the four fingers—of both his own left hand and that of the disciple into the middle of the coiled thread, and having led it around the back and back again, while both maintain the vajra-fist, he should fix it to the ground with the back of the index finger. Having adjusted the ends so as to leave no excess, the length should be twice that of the mandala.

As for the thickness, it should be one-twentieth part more than the measure of a barley grain (*yava*), which is the measure of the preceptor’s own barley grain; for it is stated in the *Abhidharma* that "a finger-joint consists of seven barley grains."

Then, with the forms of Vairocana and so forth, or the forms of Vighnantakṛt and so forth, together with the disciples who hold the marking-thread, one should first prepare the marking-threads by twisting five strands together for each; following that, one should likewise prepare the marking-threads by twisting those five together as one. Oṃ āḥ ānaya ānaya ānugataḥ sarvadharmāḥ aparaparyāya.

Reciting "āḥ | Now, enter all phenomena! āḥ | Enter! āḥ | Now, enter all phenomena! oṃ āḥ hūṃ," the master and the disciple insert the rolled thread into the four fingers, beginning from the index fingers of their left hands; they wrap it around the back [of the hand], insert and wrap it again, and then place it upon the backs of the thumb and index finger of a vajra-fist.

Having applied this to the ground, excluding the remainder up to the point of pressing down, the length of the mandala shall be twice that [of the previous measurement], and its width shall be the measure of a master’s twenty-one finger-breadths. According to the Abhidharma, seven barley grains constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).

The statement regarding the thickness of the door being one-twentieth of the eighth part of the wheel applies specifically to a mandala measuring one cubit (twenty-four finger-breadths); however, it should be understood that the measurement indicated by that same proportion applies to mandalas of two cubits and larger dimensions as well.

The explanation that the width is one-twentieth of an eighth part of the circumference refers specifically to a mandala measuring one cubit (*hasta*)—that is, twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in extent. By means of this, one should understand that mandalas with dimensions of two cubits and so forth are also to be measured accordingly.

In this way, on a circular mandala measuring six cubits, a thread of the smallest dimension should be prepared; Ānandagarbha and others maintain that this should be done proportionally in other cases as well.

Similarly, regarding a maṇḍala measuring six cubits in size, the thread for the lines should be one finger-breadth in thickness, and it should be made accordingly in other cases; this refers to [the systems of] Ānandagarbha and others.

Immediately after the turning [of the mandala], one should place the thread—smeared with scented water, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), fragrant sandalwood, and so forth, and empowered by the three syllables—into a pure vessel made of gold or other materials upon the mandala ground. Having worshipped it with flowers, incense, and other offerings, and having grasped it with the hand, one should protect it with the *sarvakarmika* mantra. Then, having looked at the sun and moon with the right and left eyes using the syllables *ma* and *ṭa*, and having stabilized the previously mentioned vajra-gaze with the syllable *maṭ*, one sprinkles it with water consecrated by the *kuṇḍali*-mantra, nectar-water, mustard seeds, and scented water.
Touched by the hand holding a vajra, one should consecrate [the thread] by reciting "Oṃ vajrasamaya sūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ" twenty-one times.

At the end of the process of joining the threads, one should smear the site of the maṇḍala with scented water, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), sandalwood, and other fragrant substances; having empowered it with the three syllables, it should be placed in a clean vessel made of gold or similar material.

Having made perfect offerings with flowers, incense, and so forth, one should touch [the object] with the hand and protect it with the *sarvakarmika* mantra. Having visualized the right and left eyes as the sun and moon from the syllables MAṂ and TĀṂ, one should stabilize them with the previously mentioned *vajradṛṣṭi*.

Having sprinkled [the thread] with water of nectar recited from the *Āvartana* mantra, along with white mustard seeds and scented water, one should touch it thoroughly with the right hand while holding a vajra and maintaining the visualization. Reciting "Oṃ vajrasamayasūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ" twenty-one times, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*).
This is the procedure for the consecration of the thread (*sūtrādhivāsanavidhi*).
Thus concludes the ritual for the consecration of the marking-thread.
